items.title: Scripps Research finds hidden structure in cell droplets, opening new drug targets

featured_image.name: What rules govern the structure of membraneless organelles?

items.description: Scientists at Scripps Research have upended a long-standing assumption in cell biology by discovering that some biomolecular condensates — the membrane-less, droplet-like compartments that cells use to organize essential processes — contain intricate internal networks of protein filaments. The findings, published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, point to new therapeutic possibilities for diseases including cancer and neurodegeneration.[1][2]

items.title: UN issues first carbon credits under Paris Agreement

featured_image.name: UN's new carbon market delivers first credits

items.description:
The United Nations on Thursday approved the first-ever carbon credits under the global carbon market established by the Paris Agreement, a milestone for international climate finance that has been more than a decade in the making — and one that has already drawn scrutiny from environmental watchdogs.

The approved credits stem from a clean-cooking project in Myanmar that distributes efficient wood-burning cookstoves to reduce household air pollution and ease pressure on local forests, the UNFCCC announced in a press release. The project, coordinated with a South Korean company, will generate credits counting toward the climate targets of both South Korea and Myanmar.[1][2]

items.title: Nvidia's record Q4 earnings send Asian markets to new highs

featured_image.name: Nvidia beats on Q4 expectations and offers better-than ...

items.description:
Asian stock markets rallied on Thursday after Nvidia reported record fourth-quarter revenue that handily topped Wall Street forecasts, easing concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom. US and European futures, however, drifted lower as investors weighed the chipmaker's results alongside lingering trade-policy uncertainty.

Nvidia posted quarterly revenue of $68.1 billion for the three months ending January 25, a 73% jump from the year-ago period and roughly $2 billion above analysts' consensus estimates. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.62, beating expectations of around $1.53. The company also guided for $78 billion in first-quarter revenue, well ahead of the approximately $72 billion Wall Street had penciled in.[1][2][3][4]

"Computing demand is growing exponentially — the agentic AI inflection point has arrived," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement, adding that customers "are racing to invest in AI compute". On the earnings call, Huang declared that "AI is here, AI is not going to go back".[5][2]

items.title: Tropical flowers blooming weeks later due to climate change, study finds

featured_image.name: Tropical flowers are blooming weeks later than they used to ...

items.description:
Tropical plants are flowering weeks or even months earlier or later than they once did as a result of climate change, according to a study of more than 8,000 plant specimens collected over two centuries. The findings, published on February 25, 2026 in the journal PLOS One, challenge the long-held assumption that tropical ecosystems — home to more than half the world's plant biodiversity — are insulated from the phenological disruptions already documented in temperate and boreal regions.[1][2]

Researchers Skylar Graves and Erin Manzitto-Tripp of the University of Colorado-Boulder analyzed museum herbarium specimens representing 33 tropical species with distinct annual flowering periods, collected between 1794 and 2024 from sites in Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, Ghana, Guinea, Thailand, and Bolivia. They found that flowering periods have shifted by an average of about two days per decade.[2][1]

items.title: Canada, South Korea sign military intel-sharing pact

featured_image.name: Canada and South Korea sign a defence agreement | CBC News

items.description:
Canada and South Korea signed a defense agreement on Wednesday focused on the exchange and protection of classified military information, as Ottawa looks to deepen ties with like-minded middle powers and Seoul positions itself to win a multibillion-dollar Canadian submarine contract.

The signing took place during the second Canada-Republic of Korea Foreign and Defence (2+2) Ministerial Meeting in Ottawa, where Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with their South Korean counterparts, Defence Minister Ahn Gyuback and Foreign Minister Cho Hyun.[1][2]

items.title: AI models used nuclear weapons in 95% of war games, study finds

featured_image.name: Advanced Nuclear War Simulator Creator Lived Near Soviet A-Bomb Test Site

items.description:
Leading AI systems from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google chose to deploy nuclear weapons in 20 of 21 simulated geopolitical crises, according to new research from King's College London that raises pointed questions about the role of artificial intelligence in military decision-making.

The study, authored by Kenneth Payne and published on the preprint server arXiv on February 16, tested three frontier large language models — OpenAI's GPT-5.2, Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4, and Google's Gemini 3 Flash — in a series of war games involving territorial disputes, competition over scarce resources, and regime survival scenarios. Over 329 turns across the 21 games, the models generated roughly 780,000 words of strategic reasoning. In none of the simulations did any model choose to surrender or fully accommodate its adversary.[1][2][3]

"The nuclear taboo doesn't seem to be as powerful for machines as for humans," Payne told New Scientist.[2]

items.title: Spanish scientists build solar panel that also harvests rain energy

featured_image.name: New tech allows solar panels to make electricity even from ...

items.description: A team of scientists in Seville has created a hybrid device that generates electricity from sunlight and rain simultaneously, turning one of renewable energy's persistent headaches — bad weather — into an additional power source. The work, published in the journal Nano Energy, introduces a thin protective film that shields fragile perovskite solar cells from moisture while also converting the kinetic energy of falling raindrops into electric current.[1][2]
